The Fawn hopping mouse (Notomys cervinus) displays a suite of life-history traits that reflect its adaptation to the arid interior of Australia. Under standard metabolic conditions measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate for this species has been recorded at 41.72 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 41.72 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, obtained from respirometry trials on captive individuals, is relatively modest for a murid rodent and likely reflects energetic economies associated with a desert existence. The ultimate wet weight for adult females reaches approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams], although field measurements indicate a range from 30 to 50 grams depending on seasonal resource availability. This body size is comparable to that of its congener the Spinifex hopping mouse, though the fawn hopping mouse tends toward the upper end of the mass spectrum within its genus. The interplay between a low metabolic rate and a moderate body mass provides insights into how this species manages the energetic demands of its unpredictable environment.

Reproductive output in Notomys cervinus is characterized by relatively small litters produced at a measured frequency. Data collected from captive breeding colonies indicate that females typically produce litters of 1 to 5 pups [N_R_i = litters of 1 to 5 pups] and can produce up to four litters each year [F_R_i = up to four litters each year], with these reproductive metrics recorded at a controlled temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], yielding an overall maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 0.04 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.04 pups per day]. This annual reproductive rate, while modest in comparison to many small rodents, is consistent with a strategy that balances offspring investment with the constraints of an arid habitat. The gestation period, also recorded at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], spans approximately 40 days [tg = approximately 40 days], with a documented range of 38 to 43 days across different captive studies. This extended gestation is noteworthy among hopping mice and may be linked to the production of relatively precocial young, as evidenced by the wet weight at birth of 2.83 grams [Wwb = 2.83 grams], a figure estimated from the closely related Notomys alexis.

The neonatal period and early developmental milestones of the Fawn hopping mouse are marked by a rapid transition to nutritional independence. Newborn pups, weighing 2.83 grams [Wwb = 2.83 grams] at birth, are altricial but develop quickly. At the standard body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 30 days [tx = 30 days], a duration that aligns with values reported for other arid-zone murids such as Notomys alexis. During this suckling period, the pups depend entirely on maternal milk, and the mother must meet both her own basal maintenance requirements and the energetic costs of lactation. This weaning age is relatively short, allowing the female to return to breeding condition swiftly in response to favorable environmental conditions. The rapid developmental pace from a birth mass of just under three grams to a fully weaned juvenile underscores the selective pressure for early independence in an environment where resource pulses are unpredictable and ephemeral.

Sexual maturation in the Fawn hopping mouse occurs after a substantial juvenile growth period under standardized thermal conditions. At 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 180 days [tp = 180 days], meaning that young animals do not reach reproductive maturity until approximately six months of age. This protracted maturation period is unusual for a rodent of its size and likely reflects the energetic investment required to attain the adult female mass of up to 50 grams [Wwi = up to 50 grams] before initiating reproduction. The delay until puberty may also serve to prevent breeding during unfavorable seasons, synchronizing first reproduction with periods of high resource abundance. In contrast to some smaller murine rodents that can mature within a few weeks, the Fawn hopping mouse exhibits a slower life-history pace that appears adapted to the boom-and-bust cycles of its desert environment, where early reproduction might be wasted if offspring cannot be adequately provisioned.

Longevity in the wild for the Fawn hopping mouse has been estimated from comparative data. At 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum lifespan is approximately 2,336 days (2336 days) [am = 2336 days], a value derived from studies of the congeneric Notomys alexis and representing a potential longevity of over six years. This is an extended lifespan for a small murid and aligns with the species' delayed sexual maturity and modest reproductive output. The oldest recorded individuals likely achieve this age through a combination of low metabolic rates and behavioral adaptations to avoid predation and thermal stress. The interplay between a late onset of puberty at 180 days [tp = 180 days] and a long potential lifespan creates a life cycle in which individuals have ample time to reproduce across multiple seasons, offsetting the risks posed by sporadic rainfall and limited food availability in the Australian desert ecosystem at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].
